title: A broadband, individually addressing two- and three-dimensional photonic integrated circuit for trapped-ion qubit control
authors: Daniel Klawson, Yiyang Zhi, Bingran You, Michael Bareian, Elijah Mossman, Chun-Yuan Fan, Arkadev Roy, Ke Sun, Jason Lee, Sung Cheol Yoon, Qiming Wu, Lai Jiang, Wenjun Ke, Weiwei Wu, Sirui Tang, Zachary Wall, Jiaxiang Wang, Louis Paul Romero, Sam Vizvary, Steven Diaz, Eric R. Hudson, Wesley C. Campbell, Hartmut Haeffner, Ming C. Wu
abstract: Trapped ions provide a high-fidelity platform for quantum information processing, yet delivery of multiple, distinct wavelengths across large networks of interaction zones remains a bottleneck. Conventional free-space light delivery lacks scalability, while on-chip grating couplers suffer from narrow operational bandwidth that increases circuit footprint and optical interfacing complexity. Here we show a broadband photonic integrated circuit capable of addressing individual ions. The circuit combines a planar waveguide lens with a micromirror fabricated using two-photon polymerization at wafer scale. This implementation can address three individual ions from $λ$ = 405 - 880 nm with -27 dB average intensity crosstalk at $5\,μ\mathrm{m}$ pitch. We trap $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ and $^{138}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ ions above such devices, characterize optical crosstalk with barium ions, and demonstrate individual repumping of calcium ions. This monolithic photonic architecture brings broadband addressing in an on-chip modality to trapped-ion technology. More generally, integrating additive manufacturing into quantum devices is poised to unlock expanded design space for implementing novel quantum architectures.
summary: The research presents a novel, monolithic photonic integrated circuit designed to overcome bandwidth limitations in trapped-ion quantum computing. By combining planar waveguides with 3D-printed micromirrors, the device achieves broadband, individually addressable light delivery across multiple wavelengths. This breakthrough significantly enhances the scalability and complexity of future trapped-ion quantum processors.
main_problem: Delivering multiple, distinct wavelengths across large networks of interaction zones for trapped-ion qubit control is a major bottleneck due to scalability issues with conventional free-space or narrow-bandwidth on-chip optics.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a monolithic photonic integrated circuit that successfully achieves broadband addressing (405–880 nm) and individual ion addressing while maintaining low optical crosstalk. This integrates 3D micro-optics fabricated via two-photon polymerization with surface electrode traps on silicon wafers.
method: The system combines lithographically defined waveguides with custom micromirrors created using two-photon polymerization (2PP) to focus light onto trapped ions ($	ext{Ca}^+$ and $	ext{Ba}^+$). Characterization involves measuring beam profiles, crosstalk, and ion repumping across the specified wavelength range.
model_or_system: The platform uses trapped ions ($	ext{Ca}^+$, $	ext{Ba}^+$) controlled by a hybrid photonic integrated circuit. This PIC integrates planar waveguides with 3D-printed micromirrors to deliver light efficiently and broadly across multiple wavelengths onto the ion trap region.
key_observables: Broadband addressing capability (405–880 nm); low optical crosstalk ($\le -27 	ext{ dB}$ at $5 \mu	ext{m}$ pitch); tight, broadband focusing profiles; successful single-ion repumping demonstration.
important_parameters: Wavelength range: 405 nm to 880 nm; Crosstalk: $-27 	ext{ dB}$; Pitch: $5 \mu	ext{m}$.
main_assumptions: The relative crosstalk profile measured at one wavelength (e.g., 455 nm) can be assumed to scale linearly for estimating coherence times at other wavelengths (e.g., 493 nm).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture, showing planar lenses and $\mu$-mirrors; beam profiles confirm tight focusing across the broadband range; crosstalk measurements quantify low signal leakage between addressed ions.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication process flow (combining LPCVD/ALD with 2PP), presents optical characterization results demonstrating broadband focusing and low crosstalk, validates ion trapping for $	ext{Ca}^+$ and $	ext{Ba}^+$, and concludes by showing individual addressing capability.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of scaling quantum processors. The integration of additive manufacturing (2PP) into established photonic platforms is a major advancement for realizing complex, scalable quantum hardware architectures.
